don't preallocate _manifest when parsing IDManifests (#2575)

Build the per-entry manifest list and the string-index mapping table
incrementally while parsing, instead of value-initializing them to the
declared/string-list size up front. This avoids an unnecessary large
allocation (and, for _manifest, a wasted default-construct + copy) when a
file declares many entries, and lets the containers reflect exactly what
was actually read.

The mapping table is now filled with push_back as the RLE runs are
expanded, so the bounds check on a decoded string index is made against
mapping.size() -- the number of indices actually populated.

Signed-off-by: Peter Hillman <peterh@wetafx.co.nz>
Co-authored-by: Cary Phillips <seabeepea@gmail.com>

Bound IDManifest uncompressed size and version-field read (#2572)

A single unvalidated 64-bit `_uncompressedDataSize` field, read directly
from an EXR file's `idManifest` attribute, was used as a `std::vector`
allocation size in `IDManifest::IDManifest(const CompressedIDManifest&)`
before decompression and before any consistency check. Depending on the
value an attacker writes into that field, an application that reads ID
manifests can be forced to either exhaust memory (an uncatchable SIGKILL,
since the vector's value-initialization physically dirties every page)
or dereference a null pointer, because a declared size of 0 makes
`uncomp.data()` null while the length check that follows decompression
still passes (0 == 0). Declared sizes of 1-3 instead produce a silent
heap out-of-bounds read of the version field. All of this is reachable
from a 343-byte file through the public, non-explicit, IMF_EXPORT
constructors `IDManifest(const CompressedIDManifest&)` and
`IDManifest(const char*, const char*)`.

Checks are added, since each failure mode is reachable on its own:

- In the `CompressedIDManifest` constructor, reject the declared
  uncompressed size before allocating anything for it if it is zero, or
  exceeds the compressed size scaled by zlib's maximum expansion ratio
  (~1032:1) -- tying the claim to bytes that must actually be present in
  the file, rather than trusting an arbitrary 64-bit value. This does
  *not* impose an absolute size ceiling: OpenEXR places no fixed limit
  on data size by default (see `Header::setMaxImageSize()`, which is
  off/unlimited unless an application opts in), so a legitimate manifest
  may be arbitrarily large provided the file actually contains that much
  compressed data.

- In `IDManifest::init()`, bounds-check the 4-byte version field read
  against the end of the buffer, exactly as the adjacent
  `readStringList()` already does for its own reads. This is the fix
  that actually matters for the null/overread cases, since `init()` is
  reachable directly through the public `IDManifest(const char*, const
  char*)` constructor without ever passing through the size check above.

- Also in `init()`, validate the per-component string index against the
  string list it ultimately selects from (`stringList[...]`), rather
  than against an intermediate container, so an out-of-range index in a
  crafted manifest is rejected with a clean exception.

Also replaced `&uncomp[0]` with `uncomp.data()`, which is well-defined
for an empty vector.

Verified by regenerating the reporter's PoC files (declared sizes of
512 MiB, 0, and 1) against `exrmanifest`: all are now rejected with a
clean exception instead of crashing or being killed by the OOM killer.
Also verified that a legitimate, honestly-compressed 300 MB manifest is
still accepted. The existing `testIDManifest` suite, which round-trips
legitimate manifests up to ~44 MB decoded, continues to pass.

Assisted-by: GitHub Copilot CLI (model: Claude Sonnet 5)

Addresses https://github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/openexr/security/advisories/GHSA-5j5m-22wr-mhc6

Signed-off-by: Cary Phillips <seabeepea@gmail.com>

coupling:
The out-of-bounds read at ImfIDManifest.cpp:578 (`stringList[mapping[stringIndex]]`) is safe only when the `mapping` table is at least as large as the range of indices admitted by the bounds check on `stringIndex`. That invariant is broken only by the COMPOSITION of the two edited commits; neither breaks it alone.

- #2575 (d6f75dc) stops value-initializing `mapping` to `stringList.size()` and builds it incrementally with push_back, so after parsing `mapping.size()` equals the number of distinct string indices the RLE map actually referenced -- which a crafted but in-contract manifest can make smaller than `stringList.size()`. Read on its own this commit is correct: it also changes the per-component bound check to test `stringIndex` against `mapping.size()`, so every `mapping[stringIndex]` access stays in bounds.

- #2572 (38d9cbf), whose purpose is tightening bounds checks on manifest reads, changes that same guard to test `stringIndex` against `stringList.size()` instead, on the reasoning that the index ultimately selects an entry from `stringList`. Read on its own (against upstream, where `mapping` is still sized to `stringList.size()`) this is a harmless, more-correct-looking tightening: there `mapping.size() == stringList.size()`, so behavior is unchanged.

Only when both land does `mapping` become shorter than `stringList` while the guard still admits any `stringIndex < stringList.size()`. A manifest whose RLE map leaves some string indices unreferenced, and whose entry then names one of those indices, reads past the end of the `mapping` heap allocation. A correct fix must reason across both commits -- either restore #2575's `mapping`-relative bound (undoing #2572's change) or re-establish a full-size `mapping` allocation (undoing #2575's change); correcting either commit's self-consistent diff in isolation leaves the bug reachable, because it lives in their interaction. Verified by execution: base (main) and the unedited batch do not fire (rc 0); a tree carrying only the #2575 edit does not fire (rc 0); a tree carrying only the #2572 edit (equivalent to upstream) does not fire (rc 0); the combined branch tip aborts under AddressSanitizer with a 4-byte heap-buffer-overflow read at ImfIDManifest.cpp:578 (rc 134).
